newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 3.

text.p: Prepared by The Broadcast Monitoring Company for Reuters

-- IMF FURY OVER CHINESE DETENTIONS The relationship between the International Monetary Fund and China is at rock bottom following the detentions of banking personnel on visits to China. The IMF were furious when Mr Yang Hong disappeared during a routine visit to Beijing with a Fund mission in December 1995. Mr Hong has since been tried in closed court for corruption and sentenced to 11 years. He is accused of taking a 12,000 dollars US bribe when at the People's Bank, China's central bank. Mr Hong is an official of the People's Bank but was on a year's secondment to the IMF at the time of the arrest, and the IMF feel that they were tricked into including him in the mission. In addition, rumours are circulating of other bizarre arrests, including that of two Hong Kong Chinese employees of SBC Warburg.

-- WATCHDOG TO ACT AS CAMELOT MISSES TARGET The National Lottery regulator, Peter Davis, is considering taking legal action against Camelot who have failed to meet targets for installing scratchcard machines in retail outlets. Camelot say the failure to meet targets was down to human error. Mr Davis decided not to revoke Camelot's operating licence because it would have meant a substantial loss of funds for the huge number of causes the lottery supports.

-- BID-TALK BLENHEIM DOUBLES PROFITS Blenheim the exhibitions group, delivered top-of-the range interim results yesterday, announcing pre-tax profits doubled at 30.7 million pounds stg. The group which has been in on and off takeover talks with Reed Elsevier and United News & Media declined to comment on bid approaches but market sources have recently suggested that the Blenheim board was willing to consider an offer at around 480p a share, after initially wanting 500p.
-- SUCCESS FOR EUROTUNNEL WITH 4 BILLION POUNDS RESCUE

PACKAGE Eurotunnel appear to have avoided the threat of insolvency after clinching a 4 billion pounds stg refinancing package with its banks. An emergency board meeting was called by Sir Alastair Morton and Patrick Ponsolle to approve the plan last night after the deal which could give the 225 banks 70 per cent or more of the equity and involves a swap of debt for equity that gives the banks an initial 49 per cent control.

-- SHARE BONANZA AWAITS NORWICH UNION VOTERS Norwich Union investors and policy holders will receive an average 500 pounds stg of free shares when the company becomes the first mutually-owned UK life insurer to float on the stock market next summer. The flotation will create a company worth between 3 and 4 billion pounds stg giving it a value similar to that of Legal & General, but smaller than the Prudential or Commercial Union.

-- CITY PRICKLY ON THISTLE PRICE Shares in Thistle Hotels have reflected City feeling that the offer was too expensive and been priced at 170p, at the bottom of the indicated range. Brierley Investments, the New Zealand company that owns 70 per cent of Thistle, Britain's second largest hotel group, said the issue had been priced to ensure the float gets away positively. The 170p offer values the group at 1.05 billion pounds stg, and will raise about 238 million pounds stg as Brierley reduces its stake to 46 per cent.

-- SHARES BREAK 4000 BARRIER The FTSE-100 index yesterday went through the 4000 barrier for the first time. The footsie finished the day 22.9 points up at 4,015.1. Equity strategists said that the confident stock market which shows growing optimism on corporate results and the strength of the economy, is also strong due to the increasing attraction of shares in comparison to gilts and to the good news continuing to come from the corporate sector.

-- CABINET IS SPLIT ON RUSH TO SELL AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL Despite growing objections from senior ministers the Treasury is trying to rush through the privatisation of the air traffic control service. Kenneth Clarke, the Chancellor, and Treasury colleagues had hoped the sale could get approval in time for it to be announced at next week's Conservative Party conference. -- RETAILERS BACK CODE FOR THIRD-WORLD SUPPLIERS A new era in high-street retailing was started yesterday when Sainsbury and the Co-op launched a project to transform their trading relationships with third-world producers. New codes of conduct will be developed by the two grocery groups in conjunction with the Fairtrade Foundation, in order to improve conditions for workers making their own-label products. The codes will be based on a third world suppliers' charter launched by the Fairtrade Foundation and backed by charities such as Oxfam and Christian Aid.
-- HTV'S BID FOR WESTCOUNTRY FALLS WELL SHORT OF 70 MILLION

POUNDS HTV has made a bid for Westcountry, the ITV licence holder for the South-west of England. One other company is believed to have expressed an interest, with Carlton or United News & Media as the most likely candidates. The bid by HTV, which reported interim profits of 6.7 million pounds stg, up 10 per cent, is thought to be less than the 70 million pounds stg Westcountry is hoping for.

-- LANG GETS REPORT ON BA ALLIANCE President of the Board of Trade, Ian Lang, received the Office of Fair Trading's report on the proposed alliance between British Airways and American Airlines yesterday. The report is believed to conclude that the alliance would operate against the public interest and should only be approved without a reference to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission if the airlines agree to surrender take-off and landing slots at Heathrow airport.
